paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.heading: Beginner Pottery
paragraphs.text: Learn to shape bowls and cups on the wheel. All clay and tools are provided, but participants should bring an apron or old clothes. Tuesdays 7–9 pm, eight weeks, £96. Maximum 8 students, so early booking is advised.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.heading: Conversational Spanish
paragraphs.text: Designed for people with some basic knowledge who want to gain confidence speaking. The tutor, a native speaker from Valencia, uses role plays based on travel situations. Mondays 6.30–8 pm, ten weeks, £85. A free trial lesson is offered on 3 March.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.heading: Digital Photography
paragraphs.text: Get the most from your camera or smartphone. Weekly assignments are posted online and discussed in class. The course ends with an exhibition of students' work in the centre's café. Wednesdays 7–9 pm, six weeks, £72. You will need your own device.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.heading: Family Cooking
paragraphs.text: Parents and children aged 8–12 cook simple, healthy meals together. The price is per pair (one adult and one child); additional children £20. Saturdays 10 am–12 noon, five weeks, £90 per pair. Please tell us about any food allergies when booking.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.heading: First Aid at Work
paragraphs.text: A one-day course leading to a certificate recognised by most employers. Suitable for anyone responsible for workplace safety. Saturday 15 March, 9 am–5 pm, £110 including lunch. Some employers will reimburse the fee, so ask your manager before booking.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.heading: Gentle Yoga
paragraphs.text: Suitable for all ages, including those recovering from injury. Mats are available, but regular students usually prefer to bring their own. Thursdays 10–11 am, ongoing. Pay £8 per class on the door; no booking required.

texts.title: Greenway Bike Share — How It Works

paragraphs.text: Greenway Bike Share has 40 docking stations across the city centre, each located no more than 500 metres from the next. Bikes can be unlocked using the Greenway app or a contactless bank card at any station terminal.

paragraphs.heading: Pricing
paragraphs.text: A single journey costs £1.50 for the first 30 minutes. After that, a charge of £1 is added for every additional 15 minutes. Members who pay an annual fee of £60 can make unlimited journeys of up to 45 minutes at no extra cost.

paragraphs.heading: Returning a bike
paragraphs.text: Bikes must be returned to a docking station. If the station you arrive at is full, the terminal will give you 15 extra minutes free of charge to reach the nearest station with space. Bikes left outside a station will result in a £50 fine.

paragraphs.heading: Safety
paragraphs.text: Helmets are not supplied, and although wearing one is not a legal requirement, we strongly recommend it. All bikes are fitted with lights that switch on automatically when the bike is moving.

paragraphs.heading: Faults and repairs
paragraphs.text: If you notice a problem with a bike, press the red button on the dock when you return it. Our maintenance team checks reported bikes within 24 hours. Riders who report three genuine faults in one month receive a free journey credit.

paragraphs.heading: Age limits
paragraphs.text: Riders must be at least 16 years old. Annual members may register up to two additional riders aged 16 or over on their account.

texts.title: Harbour Logistics — Health and Safety Guide for New Employees

paragraphs.text: Welcome to Harbour Logistics. Before you start work in the warehouse, you must complete a half-day induction run by the site safety officer. This covers emergency procedures, the safe use of equipment and the reporting of accidents. You will not be given a security pass until the induction has been completed and signed off.

paragraphs.heading: Protective clothing
paragraphs.text: High-visibility vests and safety boots must be worn at all times in the warehouse and loading areas. Boots are provided free of charge in your first week; replacements are available at half price. Office staff visiting the warehouse can borrow a vest from reception.

paragraphs.heading: Manual handling
paragraphs.text: Many injuries in our industry are caused by lifting incorrectly rather than by heavy machinery. Any item over 20 kilograms must be lifted by two people or with a mechanical aid. Staff are trained in the correct lifting technique during their second week.

paragraphs.heading: Forklift trucks
paragraphs.text: Only employees who hold a valid licence may operate a forklift truck. Pedestrians must stay within the walkways marked in green paint, and must never walk behind a reversing vehicle. Drivers sound their horn at every junction.

paragraphs.heading: Reporting incidents
paragraphs.text: All accidents, however minor, must be recorded in the accident book kept in the staff canteen. 'Near misses' — events that could have caused an injury but did not — should also be reported, using the form on the company intranet. These reports help us to identify hazards before someone is hurt.

paragraphs.heading: Fire safety
paragraphs.text: The fire alarm is tested every Monday at 10 am; at any other time you should treat it as a real emergency. Leave the building by the nearest exit and go to the assembly point in the north car park. Do not stop to collect personal belongings.

texts.title: Harbour Logistics — Applying for Internal Promotion

paragraphs.text: Harbour Logistics is committed to developing its own staff, and we aim to fill at least half of all supervisory vacancies through internal promotion. All vacancies are advertised on the staff noticeboard and the intranet for a minimum of ten working days before external candidates are considered.

To be eligible, you must have completed your probationary period and have worked for the company for at least twelve months. Employees who are subject to a formal warning are not eligible until the warning has expired.

Before applying, you are encouraged to discuss the role with the hiring manager. This informal conversation does not form part of the selection process, but it often helps candidates to decide whether the position is right for them.

Applications should be made using the internal application form rather than a CV. Your current line manager will be asked to provide a reference, so you should inform them of your application beforehand.

Shortlisted candidates are invited to an interview and, for some roles, a practical assessment. Unsuccessful internal candidates are always offered a feedback session with HR, and many go on to succeed in later applications.

Successful candidates normally move into their new role within one month. A pay rise takes effect from the first day in the new position, and there is a six-month review period during which either side may decide that the move is not working.

texts.title: The Return of the Night Train

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, overnight trains were an ordinary part of European travel. Business people, students and families would board a sleeper carriage in one capital city in the evening and wake up in another the next morning. Yet by the early 2000s the network was shrinking rapidly. Between 2000 and 2015, more than half of Europe's international night services were withdrawn, and many observers assumed that the sleeper train would soon disappear altogether.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The reasons for this decline were largely economic. Night trains are expensive to operate: a sleeper carriage carries far fewer passengers than a daytime carriage of the same length, and staff must be paid to work through the night. At the same time, the arrival of low-cost airlines meant that a flight between two major cities could often be bought for less than the price of a bed on a train. High-speed rail lines also played a part, as journeys that had once required an overnight trip could now be completed in a few hours during the day.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The turning point came, perhaps surprisingly, from a state-owned company in one of Europe's smaller countries. In 2016, when the German national operator announced that it was abandoning its sleeper services, Austrian Federal Railways decided to take over several of the routes and buy some of the rolling stock. Critics at the time described the move as a risky gamble. Within three years, however, the company reported that its Nightjet services were profitable, and passenger numbers had risen by around ten per cent a year.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Changing attitudes to the environment are widely seen as the main driver of this revival. A passenger travelling by train from Vienna to Brussels is responsible for only a small fraction of the carbon emissions produced by the same journey by air. The so-called 'flight shame' movement, which began in Sweden in 2018, encouraged travellers to reconsider short-haul flights, and surveys suggest that a growing number of people, particularly under the age of 35, are now willing to accept a longer journey if it is less damaging to the climate.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Environmental concerns alone, however, do not explain why passengers are choosing night trains rather than daytime ones. Supporters argue that the sleeper offers something no other form of transport can: it turns travelling time into sleeping time. A traveller who leaves Amsterdam at eight in the evening can arrive in Vienna in time for a morning meeting, saving both a day of travel and the cost of a hotel room. For business travellers in particular, this convenience can outweigh the lower price of a flight.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everything about the revival has gone smoothly. New routes have been delayed by a shortage of suitable carriages, since few manufacturers still produce sleeper cars and orders can take years to fulfil. Operators must also negotiate with the infrastructure companies of every country a train passes through, each with its own fees and technical rules. Some passengers, meanwhile, have complained that tickets are hard to find, as many night services are still not sold on the major international booking websites.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whether the sleeper train has a long-term future will depend largely on political decisions. Several governments have begun to offer financial support for international night services, and the European Union has identified them as one way of meeting its climate targets. Others remain unconvinced, pointing out that the money might reduce emissions more effectively if it were spent on improving local public transport. What seems certain is that the night train, which only a decade ago appeared to be a relic of the past, has once again become part of the conversation about how Europeans will travel in the future.
